description: Somos un equipo de desarrolladores de software en geolocalización, mapas interactivos, visualización 360°, y desarrollo web y mobile. Convertimos datos complejos en interfaces inmersivas de nivel aeroespacial.
summary: MARS-BLUESOFT is an interactive web application for planning a Marswalk in Jezero Crater that answers two questions: where and when it is safe to walk. It integrates, in a single view, topography from JPL Mars Trek, air and ground temperatures measured by Perseverance’s MEDA instrument (sols 1208 to 1859, covering the full Martian year), and 360° views. The user selects two points, a sol, and a departure time; a deterministic model calculates the lowest-effort route based on slope and suited walking speed, and rates each segment as Go, Caution, or No-Go according to the temperature at the time the astronaut actually reaches it. It also recommends the best departure window among the 24 hours of the Martian day. It matters because it puts crew safety first and turns data from multiple missions into decisions at a hyperlocal scale. Its layered design allows new sites and sensors to be added, such as radiation or dust. With more capacity, the application can evolve to process real-time sensor data.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

MARS-BLUESOFT answers two questions for a Marswalk in Jezero Crater: where the crew can go and when it is safe to do so. The user selects two points on the map, a sol of the Martian year (0 to 668), and a departure time in Mars Local True Solar Time (LTST). The system calculates the lowest-cost route based on terrain slope and suited walking speed, and draws it in colored segments: Go, Caution, or No-Go.

The web front end uses JPL Mars Trek as the base map. The back end, built in Python and FastAPI, works as a deterministic model. Its steps are:

  • Topography: the Mars Trek DEM is converted into elevation and slope grids. Cells that exceed the maximum slope are blocked, and the grid also defines the area scanned by NASA.
  • Temperatures: we processed MEDA (Perseverance) products from sol 1208 to sol 1859, which cover the full Martian year and its four seasons. From them we built air temperature (ATS) and ground temperature (TIRS) tables by solar longitude and local time.
  • Route: an A* search over the DEM grid.
  • Traffic light: the route is traversed cell by cell with accumulated travel time. Each cell is evaluated at the temperature of its arrival time, not the departure time, so a long route can start in Go and end in No-Go.
  • Departure window: the system tests all 24 possible hours and recommends the best one.
  • 360° views: they show the location with the routes overlaid, so the astronaut knows what to expect on arrival.

What are its benefits?

  • Safer planning: it answers where and when in a single result.
  • Decisions based on NASA-measured data, not assumed values.
  • Easy to read: a traffic light and a color-coded route instead of tables of numbers.
  • Less effort: the route avoids steep slopes that slow down walking in a suit.
  • Extensible to new sensors and sites without redesigning the tool.
  • Education and outreach: anyone can explore Mars with real NASA data.

What is the expected impact?

We want to show that data from multiple NASA missions can be turned into decisions at the hyperlocal scale of a single excursion, which is the gap that global and regional tools leave today. In the future, the tool can grow with more layers (such as radiation and dust), rock data, and a time-aware route that avoids cold segments instead of only flagging them. Because this is a prototype built with the limited resources of a hackathon, its architecture allows it to evolve toward processing real-time sensor data.

What tools, languages, and software did we use?

  • Language: Python, for the back end and data processing.
  • Libraries and frameworks: FastAPI, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and numba.
  • Maps: NASA JPL Mars Trek, in a web front end.
  • Data: MEDA from Mars 2020 Perseverance (PDS Atmospheres Node, PDS4), and the Mars Trek DEM.
  • Hardware: personal computers with a 12 GB VRAM GPU.

How is the project creative?

  • We framed it as a “hiking GPS for astronauts”: requesting a route is as simple as ordering an Uber, with two points, a sol, and a time.
  • It evaluates temperature at the arrival time of each segment, not the departure time. This changes the result, because slope lengthens the trip and that changes the temperature the astronaut encounters.
  • It turns a complex model into a traffic light that can be understood at a glance in the middle of a mission.
  • Its layered conversion means any new data enters either as a grid over the DEM or as a table by solar longitude and local time.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Safety first: blocking of excessive slopes and temperature classification for each segment.
  • Mobility in a suit: walking speed follows a Tobler-type function with a maximum of 0.8 m/s on flat ground, so slopes lengthen travel time.
  • Measured data: the temperature tables were filled only with MEDA measurements.
  • Seasonal coverage: we used the full Martian year, not a single period.
  • Transparency about limits: the cold and heat thresholds and their margin are configurable criteria, not values validated by NASA. The 0.8 m/s speed is provisional. The rock layer is already part of the cost function, but it is currently empty, so the route avoids slopes and not individual rock fields.
  • Format of use: a web application designed for the habitat, or for a tablet and PC.
